events. In the 1960s, the discovery of a new class of periodic events—microwave photons—enabled the creation of atomic clocks, which have since achieved unprecedented precision. This paper introduces a novel approach to measuring time by utilizing a different type of periodic event: the random occurrence of quantum jumps in a single, trapped ion. We demonstrate that while this method lacks the precision of atomic clocks, it offers the unique capability to measure the duration of quantum processes. Furthermore, we show that the variance in jump times provides a direct assessment of quantum uncertainty, a concept that can be experimentally verified using currently available technology. This technique also holds promise for redefining the SI second and for conducting fundamental tests of quantum mechanics and general relativity. Ultimately, our work illustrates that time can be effectively gauged by observing random processes. Such measurements are anticipated to play a pivotal role in the emerging field of quantum technologies. We conclude by proposing a new unit of time, the quantum second, to honor the significance of quantum systems in the quest to measure time. The quantum second is defined as the average interval between consecutive quantum jumps in a single ion, amounting to approximately 1.25 microwave seconds. We argue that the quantum second is more stable than the current SI second and suggest that it should be adopted as the standard unit of time in the future. We also provide an estimate of the cost required to redefine the SI second using a single trapped ion. Finally, we emphasize that the quantum second is not restricted to single ions but can be applied to any system exhibiting quantum jumps. We anticipate that this work will inspire the development of diverse quantum technologies designed to measure time with exceptional accuracy and precision. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 outlines the principles of the quantum clock; Section 3 discusses the potential applications of this clock; and Section 4 presents our conclusions. In Appendix A, we compare the quantum clock with other proposed methods for redefining the SI second, while Appendix B addresses the issue of clock drift. Additionally, we have made the quantum clock open-source, and we have successfully constructed a prototype of the device. We have also successfully demonstrated the quantum clock in an experimental setting. These findings are detailed in the reference: https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.129.100801. The quantum clock is accessible at: https://github.com/QuantumClockLab/QuantumClock. The quantum clock is open-source.

Specifically, we analyze the relationship between the geometry of the bulk and the arrangement of algebras within the boundary. We demonstrate that the commutativity of these boundary algebras is essential for successfully recovering the bulk geometry. Furthermore, we show that this principle holds true for established bulk geometries, such as those defined by the bulk reconstruction theorem and those associated with tensor networks built from perfect tensors. Finally, we apply this framework to investigate the structure of bulk geometries in noncommutative field theories. Our analysis reveals that the bulk geometry can be derived from the Hecke algebra associated with the Gelfand–Graev representation of the quantum group $U_q(SU(2))$. Additionally, we establish that the bulk geometry possesses a natural $\mathbb{Z}_2$-grading, which corresponds to the Weyl group of $U_q(SU(2))$. This grading is defined by the parity of the radial distance from the UV to the IR and aligns with the bulk geometry of noncommutative $\mathbb{C}P^2$ as described in [arXiv:1903.01220]. We also explore the implications of this grading for the emergence of spacetime. Finally, we examine the bulk geometry of a noncommutative torus and its connection to the Hecke algebra of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{C}))$. In this context, the Hecke algebra is generated by the quantum torus, and the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{C}))$ emerges as a quotient of the quantum double of the Weyl Hecke algebra. COVID-19) pandemic has triggered a surge in research regarding its potential origins, transmission, and prevention. This study aims to identify the primary source of COVID-19 outbreaks in China. Finally, the proposed complexity-based feature is shown to be robust against signal-to-noise ratio variations, offering a more resilient approach to predicting consciousness. By examining the orbital evolution of 2004 YH1, we find that it could have originated from the Maja family, a young asteroid complex situated near the 2:1 resonance with Jupiter. This scenario is supported by the fact that 2004 YH1's orbital elements align closely with those of the Maja family. Additionally, we demonstrate that the orbital evolution of 2004 YH1 can be explained by a sequence of resonances with Jupiter and the Earth, alongside the influence of the Yarkovsky effect. Learning and Data Mining: Methods and Applications* (IGI Global, 2019), offers a concise overview of ensemble learning within the context of classification tasks. It covers fundamental concepts, key algorithms, performance evaluation metrics, and the most current research methodologies in this field. Furthermore, the chapter outlines potential future research directions concerning ensembles for classification. The primary objective is to facilitate a deeper comprehension of ensemble learning for classification and to assist researchers in navigating the extensive literature on the subject. Given that the volume was published in 2019, the discussion reflects the state of the art up to that year. Readers seeking the latest advancements should consult recent survey papers, such as those by Opitz (2019), Kotsiantis et al. (2006), and Brown et al. (2007). Opitz (2019) specifically highlights the absence of empirical studies comparing ensemble performance against single classifiers, a gap this chapter aims to partially address. Additionally, Opitz (2019) notes the scarcity of recent empirical research on ensembles for regression and clustering; however, regression techniques are briefly covered in Chapter 10 and clustering methods in Chapter 11. This chapter also serves as a resource for readers interested in understanding the fundamental principles of ensemble learning for classification. Givens decomposition is essential for numerous second-order optimization techniques, including Newton's method, trust-region approaches, and quasi-Newton algorithms. However, these methods are often hindered by the high computational cost of Hessian decomposition or the substantial memory requirements of storing the full Hessian. This paper introduces a memory-efficient approach to compute the QR decomposition of the Hessian's Givens factors, facilitating the application of second-order methods in large-scale contexts. We validate this method's efficiency and accuracy across various functions, including those with zero curvature, and demonstrate its utility in second-order optimization strategies like Levenberg-Marquardt and trust-region methods. Additionally, we present a novel technique for estimating the number of significant eigenvalues of the Hessian. Experimental results indicate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art alternatives in both memory usage and computational speed. Finally, we apply this method to analyze the curvature of deep neural networks, revealing that the average number of significant Hessian eigenvalues per layer is lower than the count of network parameters per layer. These findings suggest that second-order methods could be more memory-efficient than previously thought. The code is accessible at https://github.com/lelechen/QR-Hessian-Givens. The dynamics discussed here are grounded in general representations of non-amenable groups acting on the Hilbert–Schmidt space of a amenable subgroup. Notably, we demonstrate that the Satake compactification of a semi-simple Lie group $G$ supports a transitive $G$-action precisely when $G$ possesses charm. Additionally, the existence of a transitive action of a semi-simple Lie group $G$ on a compact space $X$ of topological dimension $n$ imposes a quantitative upper bound of $n < \mathrm{charm}(G) - 1$ on $n$. This bound is achieved in numerous instances, including cases where $G$ is a rank one group, or where $G$ has rank two and acts on the Siegel upper half plane. However, this bound is not optimal in general, as the example of a transitive action of $SO_3(\mathbb{R})$ on the projective plane illustrates. Finally, we establish that the topological dimension of a $G$-orbit in the Siegel set of $G\backslash G(\mathbb{R})$ is fully determined by the multiplicity of the trivial representation of $K$ inside the isotropy representation of $K\backslash G(\mathbb{R})$, where $K$ denotes a maximal compact subgroup. This result enables us to calculate the topological dimensions of $G$-orbits in the Siegel set for all semi-simple Lie groups of rank two. These dimensions are notably small for many groups, such as $SO_3(\mathbb{R})$ and $SL_3(\mathbb{R})$, yet they are not uniform across the entire class of semi-simple Lie groups of rank two. The outcomes for $SO_3(\mathbb{R})$ align with a theorem by J. Plante, while those for $SL_3(\mathbb{R})$ were previously conjectured by S. Katok. With the rapid advancement of intelligent transportation systems, predicting future traffic conditions has become a critical task. However, accurately forecasting future states from historical data remains a significant challenge. Existing research typically models temporal dynamics using discrete-time systems, such as autoregressive networks, which often fail to fully capture the underlying dynamics of time series data. To address this limitation, we propose a novel state-space model that utilizes continuous-time dynamics to model the evolution of traffic data. This model comprises a continuous transition function and a measurement function. We employ a recurrent neural network to approximate the transition function and a feedforward neural network to approximate the observation function. Our proposed model effectively captures the underlying dynamics of traffic data and provides interpretability. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, ablation studies indicate that the model is both interpretable and efficient when dealing with irregular data. The source code is available

ARray (LOFAR) and the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) are evolving into increasingly sophisticated instruments, driven by the need for higher sensitivity, greater field of view, and improved angular resolution. These advancements are facilitated by the adoption of modern computational techniques, including machine learning and data assimilation, which are essential for managing the massive data volumes produced by these systems. This paper introduces a novel data assimilation framework designed to enhance the forward modeling of radio interferometer visibility data. The method employs a deep convolutional neural network to map visibility measurements to the corresponding sky image, conditioned on the specific interferometer's configuration. We demonstrate the application of this approach to LOFAR and MWA data, illustrating its efficacy in recovering sky images from simulated observations. Furthermore, we show that the method can identify and separate point sources from extended radio sources within the data. Ultimately, this technique offers a rapid and efficient means of generating sky images from radio interferometer measurements. This paper introduces a decentralized frequency control mechanism for power grids that leverages the frequency response capabilities of electric vehicles (EVs). By utilizing a model of an EV fleet, the study demonstrates the benefits of decentralized control in managing EVs within power grids. Furthermore, it establishes conditions ensuring that frequency deviations are minimized and that these deviations, along with the control effort, remain bounded. The proposed decentralized control scheme is validated through simulations using an EV fleet model and a network of power grids. Simulation results indicate that the decentralized approach achieves comparable performance to a centralized strategy while significantly reducing communication requirements. Additionally, the decentralized method proves more robust to variations in EV charging behavior compared to the centralized approach. These findings suggest that decentralized control is well-suited for frequency regulation in modern power grids characterized by large-scale EV adoption. Finally, the study discusses the practical implementation of this decentralized strategy in real-world grid operations. This paper presents a security analysis of the threat landscape facing CPS within the IoT era. It begins by outlining the core principles of CPS and their relationship with IoT systems. Subsequently, the study reviews potential threats and attacks, emphasizing the specific vulnerabilities of CPS. The research proposes mitigation strategies to counter CPS attacks, drawing upon existing solutions designed for IoT environments. Finally, the paper discusses open research challenges and future directions regarding CPS security. This work aims to provide a comprehensive survey of CPS threats and vulnerabilities, offering valuable insights for researchers and practitioners to enhance CPS security. To the authors' knowledge, this represents the first survey to address CPS threats from an IoT perspective. The paper is structured as follows: Section II provides background information on CPS and IoT; Section III details CPS threats and vulnerabilities; Section IV proposes mitigation strategies; Section V outlines future research directions; and Section VI concludes the paper. the solar rotation rate is typically derived from the average of observed rotation rates across different latitudes. **Aims.** This study investigates the radial variation of solar rotation by analyzing the latitudinal profiles of rotation rates within the convection zone, utilizing helioseismic data from the Global Oscillations Network Group (GONG). **Methods.** We applied the "local rotation rate" technique to determine rotation rates at various latitudes, subsequently averaging these profiles to calculate radial variations. **Results.** Our analysis reveals a shear region approximately 200 km thick at the base of the convection zone, characterized by a rotation rate roughly 10% higher than the rates in the overlying layers. **Conclusions.** This finding aligns with previous studies. **1. Introduction**
Solar differential rotation is a fundamental phenomenon, with its radial structure being a primary focus of research. The primary observational evidence for radial variations in rotation rates stems from the discovery of the tachocline—a thin shear layer at the base of the convection zone—by Christensen-Dalsgaard et al. (1981) and Thompson et al. (1986). This detection relied on helioseismic measurements of the solar surface rotation rate. Subsequent studies, such as Schou et al. (1998), utilized the same methodology to refine these findings.

The local rotation rate ($\omega(r,\theta)$) is defined as the angular velocity at a specific radius $r$ and latitude $\theta$. It is calculated by averaging the observed surface rotation rate over a narrow latitudinal band. This approach assumes that the latitudinal profile of the rotation rate remains relatively constant throughout the convection zone. However, this assumption is not guaranteed, and deviations can lead to significant errors in estimating radial variations.

In this study, we examine how such variations affect the determination of radial rotation rate changes. We demonstrate that the thickness of the tachocline and the rotation rate difference at its base remain independent of the specific latitudinal profiles employed for averaging. Additionally, we present a method for estimating the tachocline's thickness and the magnitude of the rotation rate difference at its base.

This study investigates the potential of such a signal to constrain dark matter (DM) properties, specifically focusing on ultralight bosonic DM and self-interacting DM. For bosonic DM, we demonstrate that the pulsar timing array (PTA) background can be generated by scalar DM through the decay of heavy dark matter particles, while the PTA's upper limit on the background amplitude imposes a constraint on the heavy DM decay rate. Additionally, we show that a stony core within a supermassive black hole (SMBH), formed by self-interacting DM, can produce a stochastic gravitational wave background detectable by PTAs. This signal arises from the collapse of the DM core and the subsequent oscillation of the SMBH due to its self-interaction. We derive the expected amplitude and spectral index for this signal and illustrate how PTA observations can distinguish it from the universal power-law background. Furthermore, we find that this scenario can be compatible with the observed 5.5-solar-mass binary black hole merger event, GW190814. Finally, we highlight that PTA searches for such a stony core offer a novel method to detect self-interacting DM. In summary, PTAs provide a powerful tool for constraining the parameter space of ultralight bosonic DM and self-interacting DM, as well as for probing the stochastic gravitational wave background. These searches are complementary to those conducted by space-based and ground-based interferometers. We anticipate that future PTA observations will yield stronger constraints on these dark matter models. This study examines the impact of solar rotation on the distribution of magnetic field strength in photospheric flux tubes, utilizing high-resolution observations from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) aboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). We analyzed 10 years of HMI data from 2010 to 2019, employing a novel method to determine the inclination angle of flux tubes relative to the solar surface. By comparing active regions across two distinct solar rotation periods—the solar minimum (2010–2014) and the solar maximum (2015–219)—we investigated how magnetic field strength varies with rotation angle. Our results indicate that the distribution of magnetic field strength is not uniform with respect to the rotation angle. Specifically, we observed a significant increase in magnetic field strength at the solar maximum compared to the solar minimum. Furthermore, the distribution of magnetic field strength exhibits a clear dependence on the inclination angle of the flux tubes. These findings suggest that solar rotation plays a pivotal role in shaping the distribution of magnetic field strength within photospheric flux tubes. Additionally, we found that the inclination angle distribution is asymmetric around the equator, with a higher frequency of magnetic field strength values at the ascending node than at the descending node. This asymmetry is more pronounced during the solar maximum than during the solar minimum. Finally, we identified a strong correlation between the inclination angle and the magnetic field strength, indicating that flux tubes with a smaller inclination angle possess a higher magnetic field strength. These results align with previous studies on the evolution of active regions. Overall, our findings suggest that solar rotation significantly influences the distribution of magnetic field strength in photospheric flux tubes. Liouville conformal field theory characterized by generalized structure constants. This study examines specific aspects of their correlators, with a primary focus on three-point functions. By utilizing Dotsenko-Fateev contour integrals within an annulus representation, the three-point functions are linked to hypergeometric functions. Furthermore, we derive a closed-form expression for the ratio of any two components of the vector of structure constants, classifying them as hypergeometric functions of type ${}_3F_2$. Finally, we explore the connection between these CFT structure constants and the Racah-Wigner $6j$-symbols associated with the quantum group $U_q(sl_2)$. Additionally, we demonstrate that the correlation functions of Toda conformal field theory can be realized as matrix elements of the quantum group. This relationship enables the derivation of a novel formula for the matrix elements of the quantum group, expressed in terms of hypergeometric functions. Consequently, we establish a link between the $6j$-symbols of the quantum group and those of the classical Lie algebra. Finally, we illustrate the consistency of our findings with the $q$-Kostant formula regarding the decomposition of tensor products of irreducible representations of the quantum group. Additionally, we demonstrate that the $6j$-symbols of the quantum group can be realized as matrix elements of the Wigner $D$-matrices. This connection allows us to derive a formula expressing the matrix elements of the Wigner $D$-matrices through hypergeometric functions. As a significant consequence, we obtain a relationship between the Clebsch-Gordan coefficients and the $6j$-symbols of the quantum group. This relationship serves as a quantum analogue to the corresponding relation in Lie algebra representation theory. Finally, we establish a novel formula for the $6j$-symbols of the quantum group using $q$-Gauss hypergeometric series of type ${}_4F_3$. This formula exhibits a remarkable symmetry with respect to its arguments, exhibiting a high degree of invariance under permutations of its indices. This level of symmetry is rare in the $6j$-symbols of quantum groups and underscores the naturalness of this approach. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this formula aligns with the fundamental properties of the $6j$-symbols of the quantum group. In conclusion, we have successfully derived a formula for the $6j$-symbols of the quantum group that exhibits significant symmetry. ho Ophiuchus cluster exhibits a peculiar morphology, featuring a collimated outflow directed toward the cluster center and a broad, fan-like structure oriented perpendicularly. This anomaly is likely caused by the interaction between S1's stellar wind and the ambient medium. We propose a model in which the star's collimated wind, driven by magnetic fields, penetrates the dense wind from an embedded protostellar core, creating a collimated jet, while the core's wider wind is deflected by the stellar wind to form the observed fan-like shape. This configuration is consistent with the observed spectral energy distribution (SED) of S1, which displays a broad infrared excess indicative of a protostellar core. Furthermore, the model aligns with the observed outflow direction, which points toward a nearby Class 0/I protostar, RHO Oph MM1. The similarity in the spatial orientation of the outflow and the protostar's elongation suggests that the outflow is indeed driven by Rho Oph MM1. Finally, we discuss the implications of this finding for understanding the formation of collimated outflows in young stellar objects. While it is typically applied during the forward pass, we introduce it into backpropagation to further reduce the training expenses of a single model. Our approach, called Backward Weight Sharing (BWS), applies a differentiable function to one model's gradients during backpropagation to generate another model's gradients. This effectively halves the computational and memory requirements for training the models, with minimal impact on training accuracy. Furthermore, BWS can be combined with the forward pass to create a compact two-tower architecture, enabling the simultaneous training of two models in the forward pass and one pair of models in the backward pass, thereby reducing both training time and memory usage by nearly 75%. We validate the efficacy of this method across various tasks, including image classification, object detection, and instance segmentation. Additionally, we explore a secondary application where BWS facilitates the training of a model using a small dataset by leveraging gradients from a model trained on a larger dataset. Finally, we demonstrate that the compact models produced by BWS can be expanded to match the performance of their non-shared counterparts with negligible accuracy loss. ### 1. Introduction

Dimensionality reduction is a critical challenge in data analysis, with the ultimate goal of creating interpretable representations of data points. This capability is essential for downstream tasks such as visualization and classification. While numerous dimensionality reduction techniques exist, many are either too complex for practical application or fail to produce interpretable outcomes. The Locally Linear Embedding (LLE) algorithm exemplifies this limitation; although it achieves low reconstruction error by approximating data points as linear combinations of their nearest neighbors, it does not ensure that points with similar local structures remain close in the reduced space.

In contrast, the neighborhood component analysis (NCA) algorithm [1] offers a promising approach by directly optimizing for local structure preservation. It calculates the probability that a point $x_i$ is classified as $x_j$ based on a trained SVM, thereby retaining local information. By minimizing the difference between these probabilities in the original and reduced spaces, LLE can be adapted to retain local structure. This concept forms the basis of the popular visualization algorithm, t-SNE [2].

t-SNE operates by converting high-dimensional data into a probability distribution and embedding it into a low-dimensional space that similarly represents a probability distribution. To achieve this, the algorithm computes a Gaussian distribution for high-dimensional points and a Student's t-distribution for low-dimensional points. The core mechanism involves minimizing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between these two distributions. A key feature of t-SNE is its adaptive neighborhood size, controlled by the perplexity parameter. This parameter is derived from the data's inherent dimensionality

This study examines the GUP's impact on the thermodynamics of Reissner-Nordström black holes and their anti-de Sitter counterparts. By incorporating GUP corrections, the Bekenstein-Hawking temperature is modified, leading to a phase transition between these black holes and thermal radiation. Furthermore, the analysis explores the effects of GUP on the Hamiltonian of the black hole system, revealing that the energy spectrum is no longer continuous but becomes discrete. Consequently, the black hole's Hamiltonian is determined through the summation of these discrete energy levels. The findings indicate that the total energy of the black hole is significantly affected by GUP; for instance, the Anti-de Sitter black hole's energy can be reduced by approximately 10% or more. These results suggest that GUP plays a crucial role in black hole thermodynamics and energy calculations. Additionally, the discrete energy spectrum offers a potential resolution to the information loss paradox, as information could be encoded within the discrete states of the black hole. This work underscores the significance of GUP in refining our understanding of black hole properties and thermodynamic behavior. Finally, the study briefly extends these concepts to cosmology, examining the Big Bang scenario under the framework of GUP. The results demonstrate that GUP can prevent the universe from collapsing into a singularity, offering further insights into the early universe's structure. Overall, this research highlights the profound implications of GUP in both black hole physics and cosmological theories. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the GUP and revisits the thermodynamics of Reissner-Nordström black holes in anti-de Sitter space. Section 3 investigates the phase transition between Reissner-Nordström black holes and thermal radiation by modifying the temperature via GUP. Section 4 analyzes the black hole's Hamiltonian by considering discrete energy states based on GUP. Section 5 discusses the impact of GUP on the black hole's energy. Section 6 explores the resolution of the information loss paradox using the discrete energy spectrum. Section 7 applies GUP to the Big Bang scenario. Section 8 concludes the study and outlines future research directions. Our findings indicate that while the self-energy for an infinite system remains insensitive to the impact of a single defect, it is highly dependent on a system of defects. We illustrate this behavior using a scenario where every second atom is substituted with a "superatom." In this case, the system's self-energy can be exactly represented as a rational function, allowing us to examine how defect strength and spacing affect electron transmission. Furthermore, we explore the potential of this self-energy representation in designing molecular devices. Specifically, we demonstrate that these systems can function as molecular transistors, where the defect-induced self-energy modulates conductance in response to a gate voltage. Additionally, we show that such systems can act as dimers with tunable bond lengths, serving as effective low-pass filters. Finally, we confirm that these structures can operate as transistors with current gain exceeding unity. This research provides a theoretical framework for investigating the electronic properties of molecular wires and rings, with potential applications in quantum computing. The methodology is also applicable to other lattice systems featuring weak disorder. Our results offer a deeper understanding of how defects affect electron transport in molecular wires, which is crucial for the development of nanoscale electronic devices. We believe this study will stimulate further investigations into the electronic characteristics of molecular rings and wires. This paper introduces a quantum learning framework capable of training quantum neural networks to perform quantum classification tasks. We establish convergence theorems to demonstrate that our quantum neural network can effectively learn the target quantum classifier. Furthermore, we provide an explicit learning algorithm for data linearly separable in the Bloch sphere and calculate the corresponding learning complexity. Our findings indicate that the number of layers in the quantum neural network depends on the dimension of the input quantum state. Additionally, we illustrate that our learning complexity is contingent upon the approximation error. Finally, we compare our learning complexity with that of Grover's quantum algorithm regarding data linear separability. These results suggest that quantum neural networks offer a viable approach to learning quantum classifiers. This study also holds relevance for data separable in the Bloch sphere and for quantum operators that are eigen-operator separable. We anticipate that these findings will contribute to the advancement of quantum machine learning. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 outlines the preliminaries; Section 3 presents the quantum learning framework; Section 4 details the convergence theorems and the learning algorithm; Section 5 discusses the learning complexity; and Section 6 presents the conclusion. Building on prior research regarding eigenvalue localization, we derive lower bounds for the distance between distinct eigenvalues, demonstrating that these bounds approach zero as the domain progressively resembles a sphere. Furthermore, we establish that the asymptotic rate at which these lower bounds vanish is independent of the specific domain, provided it remains sufficiently close to a sphere. This result suggests a universal behavior in perturbed Steklov problems, contrasting with the well-documented divergence of condition numbers in other problems involving domains close to spheres. The primary methodology employed is microlocal analysis. Additionally, we present a general framework for perturbed Steklov problems on manifolds with boundaries, enabling the derivation of similar lower bounds on the condition number for a broad class of perturbations. The findings in this paper are particularly pertinent to the case where the boundary perturbation is defined by a graph. As an application, we analyze the stability of distinct eigenvalues for perturbed Steklov problems on graphs, proving that the condition number for graphs perturbed by small $C^2$ deformations is bounded from below by a term proportional to the square root of the perturbation size. This bound is sharp and remains independent of the domain's specific characteristics. The primary instrument used to achieve this result is the explicit construction of localized eigenfunctions. Our findings indicate that perturbed Steklov problems on graphs exhibit stability properties analogous to those observed on manifolds. Finally, we provide a comprehensive comparison between the results on graphs and those on manifolds. While vector field methods have previously been employed to address Vlasov equations with specular reflection, this work extends those approaches to incorporate the Poisson equation. A primary challenge arises because the compatibility conditions required for global existence are not fulfilled in bounded domains. To overcome this, we introduce a novel method for deriving a priori estimates of the Poisson potential using vector fields. This approach avoids the need for Lagrange multipliers and relies on a new identity for vector field derivatives under specular reflection, which is of independent significance. Furthermore, vector fields are applied to derive $L^2$ estimates for the distribution function, thereby proving global existence. As a secondary contribution, we also demonstrate the convergence of the corresponding linearized system. This result is achieved by deriving a weight function that satisfies specific properties, allowing us to prove the global existence of a positive solution to an integral equation, which subsequently enables the derivation of a priori estimates. Finally, we provide a comprehensive overview of vector field methods applicable to the Vlasov equation under specular reflection. This includes a unified framework for deriving $L^2$ estimates and proving the global existence of classical solutions across various settings, such as periodic domains, unbounded domains with subcritical growth, and bounded domains with Neumann boundary conditions. Additionally, we derive uniform estimates for the distribution function in these contexts. Our findings offer a pathway to extend vector field methods to other coupled kinetic-macroscopic systems, such as the Vlasov-Maxwell and Boltzmann-Poisson systems. This could facilitate the global existence of classical solutions in these systems, either directly or by adapting the vector field method to their specific requirements. Furthermore, our vector field method is designed to handle general non-linear terms, making it applicable to more general kinetic equations. In this regard, we demonstrate that the method can address the global existence of classical solutions for the Vlasov equation with general nonlinear interactions. These results are derived by proving the existence of a positive solution to an integral equation and obtaining appropriate a priori estimates. Consequently, this paper offers a comprehensive and unified framework for global existence using vector fields in kinetic equations with nonlinear interactions. Finally, we illustrate the application of these methods to the Vlasov equation with nonlinear interactions in both periodic and unbounded domains exhibiting subcritical growth. Our findings indicate that the nonlinear term imposes no additional difficulties in deriving a priori estimates for the distribution function in both cases. However, the mechanisms governing their formation and the nature of their microstructure remain poorly understood. This study employs in situ confocal microscopy to track the dynamics of a silica particle suspension gelled by gravity, revealing that the resulting structure consists of dense clusters connected by sparse bridges. The ratio of bridged to clustered particles is directly proportional to the gravitational stress applied during gelation. Furthermore, the gel's mechanical properties are found to be independent of the initial concentration of free particles. These findings are modeled using a modified Maxwell framework, which incorporates the relaxation of free particles to explain the observed linear viscoelastic properties. Overall, these results provide a predictive framework for tailoring the mechanical properties of gelled systems across a wide range of concentrations. Hall's condition, which states that the union of neighborhoods for any group of agents must be at least as large as the group itself. While this condition is straightforward to verify for a single agent, it becomes difficult to check in dynamic environments with multiple agents. This paper introduces a novel distributed algorithm that enables agents to verify and maintain Hall's condition in real-time. The algorithm operates in two phases: first, agents identify their "excess neighborhood" and "excess agent set" through a distributed process; second, they calculate a matching that pairs every agent in the excess agent set with a unique node from the excess neighborhood. By continuously running this algorithm, agents can confirm that Hall's condition holds. The proposed method is fully distributed, meaning agents only need local information to execute the steps. Furthermore, the algorithm is provably correct and terminates in finite time. Finally, we demonstrate how this approach can be applied to monitor the connectivity of multi-agent systems. Simulations are provided to illustrate the algorithm's performance. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/HallsCondition. To better understand these communication patterns, we analyzed over 1.5 million commits from GitHub, identifying more than 100,000 pairs of developers who collaborated on the same code. By comparing these empirical communication patterns against a null model, we found that while collaboration frequency and pair stability are similar to random expectations, the diversity of collaborators is significantly lower. This suggests that developers tend to work repeatedly with a small, familiar group of peers. Furthermore, our results indicate that frequent collaborators are more likely to share a common institutional affiliation. Finally, we observed that the rate at which collaboration pairs dissolve is independent of the number of years the pair has been working together. These findings offer valuable insights for tools and systems designed to facilitate developer communication. Specifically, they highlight the need for systems to proactively suggest collaborators beyond a user's immediate circle, as well as to provide access to the full history of a developer's collaborative relationships. However, in certain systems, this balance is disrupted by a strong magnetic field, which suppresses the generation of eddies with scales smaller than the inverse Alfvén wavenumber. This study investigates the energy spectrum of such geostrophic turbulence through both direct numerical simulations and an analytical model. In the Alfvén wavenumber range, the energy spectrum exhibits a $k^{-3}$ scaling, whereas at larger scales, it follows a $k^{-5/3}$ law, consistent with Rossby wave theory. We demonstrate that the former regime corresponds to an Alfvénic regime, where the energy flux is governed by the relative phase of Alfvén waves traveling in opposite directions along the magnetic field. At larger scales, the phase difference is determined by the system's nonlinearity. Furthermore, we show that the spectral exponent in the inertial range can be controlled by adjusting the ratio of the forcing scale to the Alfvén wavenumber, resulting in a continuous spectrum of $-5/3 < p < -7/3$ for a spectrum of $E(k) \sim k^{-p}$. This control mechanism is also observed in the energy spectrum of the solar wind. Our findings indicate that geostrophic turbulence displays distinct characteristics when a strong background magnetic field is present. These results may offer a new perspective for understanding geostrophic turbulence in geophysical and astrophysical contexts. Additionally, our model provides a framework for calculating the energy spectrum of geostrophic turbulence, which could aid in interpreting data from direct numerical simulations and laboratory experiments. Finally, our findings may offer a new explanation for the observed $k^{-3}$ scaling in the solar convection zone. This study investigates whether such emission can be generated within the ionized interstellar medium (ISM) of a starburst galaxy, specifically using M82 as a case study. We employ a model of M82's ionized ISM, constructed from H$\alpha$ and H$\beta$ maps, to analyze the conditions necessary for radio wave generation. By applying a two-fluid plasma model, we calculate the frequencies of coherent radio waves and their associated radio sputtering rates. Our findings indicate that in the ionized ISM of M82, the conditions for generating coherent radio waves are not met. However, these conditions are satisfied in the dense molecular clouds and the outflow, where the two-fluid instability produces radio waves at frequencies between 10 and 100 MHz. These emission regions are located near the ionization fronts of HII regions and around the supernova-driven outflow. We conclude that the ionized ISM in starburst galaxies is generally too dilute to support coherent radio wave generation, except in the immediate vicinity of ionization fronts. Furthermore, we suggest that the outflow from M82 may be responsible for the low-frequency radio waves detected from this galaxy. While robustness is a fundamental component of decision making, especially under uncertainty, it remains difficult to assess and compare across different strategies. investigate the low-temperature characteristics of the one-dimensional Heisenberg antiferromagnet with weak easy-axis anisotropy. Our results indicate that easy-plane interactions induce a quantum critical point at an infinitesimal anisotropy value, causing the spin gap to vanish as the ground state transitions from gapped to gapless. We further demonstrate that this gapless state corresponds to a dimerized version of the Haldane spin liquid, featuring an antiferromagnetic correlation decay exponent of $z=1.67(2)$. Additionally, we observe that the spin correlation length scales with anisotropy in a power-law fashion, a finding that aligns with recent experimental data on Yttrium Barium Copper Oxide. Finally, we propose that the observed power-law behavior can be accounted for by a conformal field theory with a central charge of $c=1$. Furthermore, we examine the scaling of the spin correlation length with system size in the absence of anisotropy, observing that even for a system size of $L=128$, the antiferromagnetic correlation length remains finite, with the gap decreasing as $L^{-1.3(1)}$. These findings suggest that the gapless state is not the dimerized Haldane spin liquid, but rather a distinct gapless phase that emerges abruptly at the quantum critical point. This phase is likely a conformal field theory with $c=1$ and a non-Haldane ground state, where the antiferromagnetic correlation length diverges as $z=1.3(1)$. We also discuss the potential for this phase to be realized in spin-1 chains with alternating site anisotropies. By employing the Jordan-Wigner transformation, we show that the Hamiltonian can be mapped to a free fermion model, where the ground state is identified as a Fermi sea. This implies that the proposed phase is unique to Hamiltonians where the spin-1 Hamiltonian density can be expressed as the sum of two Hermitian operators. We also address the possibility of this phase occurring in other spin-1 models, such as the $SU(2)$-symmetric Heisenberg model with next-nearest-neighbor interactions. Finally, we present the argument that the ground state of the Heisenberg antiferromagnet with next-nearest-neighbor interactions is a non-Haldane gapless phase, supported by evidence from both exact diagonalization and large-scale density matrix renormalization group studies. In the ultraviolet regime, the theory aligns with Yang-Mills theory, while in the infrared, it remains consistent with a gauge-invariant extension of the Higgs mechanism. This study examines the effects of both axisymmetric and non-axisymmetric magnetic fields on the pulsational characteristics of white dwarfs, neutron stars, and main-sequence stars. We determined the adiabatic index for these stars under the influence of magnetic fields and calculated the gravitational energy of the stars when magnetic effects are considered. Furthermore, we analyzed how magnetic fields influence the gravitational energy density, the energy density of the magnetic field itself, and the energy density of the stress tensor. Our findings indicate that the energy density of the magnetic field is negligible compared to the star's total energy density. alline La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$NiIrO$_{6}$ were investigated using X-ray diffraction, specific heat, magnetization, and susceptibility measurements. Results indicate that for $x \leq 0.2$, the material adopts a monoclinic structure with space group $C2/m$, whereas higher Sr concentrations ($x \geq 0.4$) stabilize an orthorhombic structure (space group $Pbnm$). The Ni$^{2+}$ ion in this system is a $d^8$ configuration with a ground state of $^3$A$_2$. At low temperatures, the specific heat and susceptibility data reveal a spin anisotropy where the $c$-axis is the easy axis and the $a$- and $b$-axes are the hard axes. Furthermore, the magnetic susceptibility of the $x=0$ sample exhibits a minimum at $T_{min}=10$ K, suggesting the onset of short-range magnetic order. Finally, the specific heat and magnetization measurements indicate that the long-range antiferromagnetic ordering temperature is approximately 5 K. These findings are consistent with a theoretical model describing a two-dimensional ferromagnetic order within an antiferromagnetic lattice. Additionally, the specific heat of the $x=0.1$ sample displays a broad peak at 10 K, which may be attributed to a spin glass transition. This study provides the first comprehensive characterization of a full series of solid-solution La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$NiIrO$_{6}$ single crystals. Furthermore, the observed spin anisotropy and the potential spin glass transition in d$^8$ Ni$^{2+}$ compounds represent significant findings. These results offer a foundation for exploring novel magnetic phenomena in this class of materials. , we have created a large-scale, high-resolution (100 $\mu$m) 3D-printed phantom for brain MRI. This phantom is engineered to facilitate the development of novel imaging sequences and image reconstruction algorithms, specifically targeting the imaging of small lesions. We demonstrate that MRI can successfully visualize 3D printed objects with a voxel size of 100 $\mu$m x 100 $\mu$m x 1 mm under these conditions. Utilizing a 7T scanner, we achieved 3D imaging of a phantom containing 1 mm x 1 mm x 1 mm printed cubes with a 100 $\mu$m isotropic voxel resolution in approximately 10 minutes. Furthermore, we successfully reconstructed 2D images with a 100 $\mu$m isotropic voxel within 10 seconds by applying a novel 3D image reconstruction method. These findings indicate that 3D printing serves as a highly effective tool for validating and advancing ultra-high field MRI, enabling the visualization of minute lesions at 100 $\mu$m isotropic resolution. This capability holds significant promise for early-stage detection of various diseases, including brain tumors, in the future. Additionally, the 3D printed cubes can function as fiducial markers to enhance the accuracy of image registration in multimodal imaging. We have made the phantom and its design files publicly accessible to support further research and development. Under specific conditions, the trajectory of a robot with negative work capability on such terrain exhibits a Zeno behavior, characterized by an infinite sequence of discrete slip events within a finite time interval. We also examine the sensitivity of $R_\Sigma$ to various Standard Model long-distance effects, including final-state interactions, hadronic form factors, and meson mixing. Finally, we illustrate that the observable can detect new physics scenarios, such as those arising from non-universal new gauge bosons. These findings suggest that future measurements of $R_\Sigma$ will offer a complementary test of the Standard Model, with the potential to reach a precision of approximately 1%. Our analysis indicates that, in the near future, ATLAS could achieve a precision of roughly 10%, while LHCb could achieve a precision of about 1%. These results are expected to be achievable using existing datasets. We conclude that the $R_\Sigma$ observable offers a robust method for testing the Standard Model and searching for new physics. **I. INTRODUCTION**

Interconnected nonlinear systems are prevalent in numerous practical applications, including chemical plants, robotic systems, and power grids. These systems typically consist of multiple subsystems interacting through nonlinear couplings. A significant practical issue arises when these interconnected nonlinearities are unknown, often due to complex system dynamics or modeling difficulties. Consequently, developing control strategies that can effectively handle such unknown interactions is crucial.

This similarity suggests that the hadronization mechanism in $pp$ collisions at this energy is comparable to that in small systems within the quark-gluon plasma. 20% of patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) exhibit signs of pulmonary vascular disease, a finding that may influence the efficacy of antifibrotic medications. **Objectives:** This study aimed to evaluate the prevalence of pulmonary vascular disease in IPF patients and analyze its relationship with disease severity and clinical outcomes. **Methods:** We conducted a retrospective analysis of 100 IPF patients who underwent high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) and pulmonary function testing (PFT). The cohort was divided into two groups: those with evidence of pulmonary vascular disease (PVD-IPF) and those without (PVD--IPF). **Results:** The overall prevalence of PVD in IPF was 20%. Patients in the PVD-IPF group demonstrated more severe disease, characterized by lower forced vital capacity (FVC) and carbon monoxide diffusion capacity (DLCO), a higher FVC/DLCO ratio, and a greater proportion of severe fibrosis on HRCT. Additionally, PVD-IPF patients had a higher 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) and a lower 6MWD/FVC ratio. **Conclusions:** PVD-IPF patients present with more advanced disease severity, as evidenced by reduced FVC and DLCO, an increased FVC/DLCO ratio, and a higher frequency of severe fibrosis on HRCT. These findings suggest that PVD-IPF patients may experience a slower decline in lung function compared to those without PVD. **Keywords:** Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; Pulmonary vascular disease; Severity; Clinical outcomes.

We say that $G$ is $R$-homogeneous if, for every pair of edges $\{u_1,v_1\}$ and $\{u_2,v_2\}$ in $G$, the existence of $R(u_1,u_2)$ implies the existence of $R(v_1,u_2)$ and $R(v_2,u_1)$. A graph is $r$-regularly homogeneous (or simply homogeneous) if it is $R$-homogeneous where $R(x,y)$ holds precisely when the distance between $x$ and $y$ is at most $r$. The study of $r$-regularly homogeneous graphs is motivated by the investigation of strongly $R$-regular graphs, defined as graphs where, for any adjacent vertices $x$ and $y$, the distance between their neighbors is either $r$ or $R$. In this work, we demonstrate that the complete bipartite graph $K_{n,n}$ is $r$-regularly homogeneous if and only if $r \in \{0,1,2\}$. Furthermore, we establish that the incidence graph of a finite strongly $R$-regular graph is $r$-regularly homogeneous for all $r > 2$. Finally, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition for an $r$-regularly homogeneous graph to be strongly $R$-regular. Additionally, we examine other classes of graphs, such as Cayley graphs, that possess the $r$-regularly homogeneous property. Specifically, we show that the incidence graph of a finite symmetric block design is $r$-regularly homogeneous if and only if the design is a projective plane of order $k$, where $R(x,y)=k$ or $k+1$. Consequently, we derive that the incidence graph of a finite symmetric block design is strongly $R$-regular if and only if the order $k$ is at most $2$. This result implies that no strongly $R$-regular graph exists with an order of $k^2+2k+1$ when $k > 2$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that no strongly $R$-regular graph of order $k^2+2k+1$ exists for $k > 2$, except for the case where $k=3$ and $R=10$. In this specific scenario, we provide a complete classification of such graphs

This approach, known as the Generalized Linear Mixed Model (GLMM), functions by treating the observed covariates as realizations of a higher-dimensional vector that includes both observed and unobserved (latent) components. This study investigates the impact of high-energy irradiation on the chemical composition of a protoplanetary disk around the young star TW Hya, utilizing a coupled model that integrates X-ray/UV heating with chemical evolution. This model offers a straightforward depiction of radiation friction as a dissipative force, where the dissipative coefficient encapsulates the characteristics of emitted particles. Furthermore, this approach facilitates a comparison with the classical radiation reaction force. The worldline method is extended to strong fields by introducing an external field term within the exponent of the worldline propagator. Finally, the resulting expression for radiation friction is derived for the case of a constant electric field. This work serves as a foundation for developing a general, model-independent description of radiation friction applicable to arbitrary external fields. Additionally, it provides a viable alternative to the conventional worldline path integral formulation for strong fields, which often encounters convergence challenges. The proposed method is also extensible to relativistic quantum gases and systems involving spin degrees of freedom. As a demonstration of this approach, we calculate the radiation friction force for a relativistic particle in a constant, uniform electric field. In this scenario, the force is described by a damping coefficient that depends on the density of emitted photons and an intercept representing the non-dissipative component of the radiation reaction. For a static field, the damping coefficient is proportional to the square of the Schwinger parameter, which governs pair production. This indicates that radiation friction becomes significant when particle creation is suppressed, a regime where the standard Landau-Lifshitz approximation fails. In this context, radiation friction acts to enhance pair production. Furthermore, the derived expression for radiation friction in a time-dependent electric field aligns with the findings of Suraev and Ternov. We also examine the implications of these results for relativistic plasmas. Specifically, in a plasma with a temperature exceeding the Schwinger limit, the photon-induced damping coefficient is non-zero, leading to an amplification of pair production. This suggests that in ultra-high-temperature astrophysical environments, such as the core of a neutron star, pair production could be amplified by the radiation friction force. These findings may offer a viable explanation for the anomalous thermal conductivity observed in neutron stars. Additionally, we explore the potential impact of this radiation friction force on the dynamics of the early universe. We demonstrate that the exponential expansion of the universe can trigger pair production through radiation friction, a mechanism that could have played a crucial role in the early stages of the universe. This study examines the topology of a specific network class: those formed by the superposition of two or more random graphs. We analyze how the spectral and structural metrics of these superposed networks vary as functions of the number of components and their individual topological traits. Notably, our findings indicate that topological features of the superposed network can be significantly distinct from those of each constituent graph. Furthermore, we explore the potential of this approach to unravel the structure of unknown networks, proposing that decomposing a random superposition into its original components may yield insights into the mechanisms driving the formation of such networks. Finally, we outline a method for identifying these constituent components. We validate this decomposition method across various scenarios, including cases where graph superpositions are weighted, and we illustrate its application to real-world networks, including a case study on a primate brain. Ultimately, we argue that networks formed by the superposition of random graphs represent a category worthy of dedicated research.

the formation of the air-water interface in open containers. This study examines how varying wall contact angles influence the development of capillary waves. We demonstrate that the curvature of the meniscus at the wall, which is independent of the central column's curvature, serves as a more accurate representation of wall effects. Furthermore, we derive a theoretical model for the dispersion relation of capillary waves that incorporates this wall curvature. Our findings indicate that when the radius of the central column is significantly smaller than the capillary length, the influence of the contact angle on wave frequency is minimal. However, if the container's radius is comparable to the capillary length, the wall curvature has a substantial impact, causing the wave frequency to increase as the container becomes more vertical. These results are supported by numerical simulations. Finally, we suggest that the theory presented here can be applied to analyze the behavior of liquid columns in microfluidic devices. To enhance the precision of parallel robot manipulators, researchers have developed various algorithms and techniques, including the use of compliant serial chains to mitigate the drawbacks of traditional rigid mechanisms. This study introduces a novel hybrid parallel-serial robot featuring a 3-DOF parallel mechanism and a 1-DOF compliant chain. The research focuses on analyzing the robot's workspace and kinematic performance. First, the workspace is determined using the analytical method, followed by an evaluation of kinematic metrics—specifically condition number, dexterity index, and condition number of the Jacobian transpose—throughout the workspace. Subsequently, a multi-objective optimization algorithm is employed to identify the optimal workspace region by minimizing the count of singular and near-singular configurations alongside the condition number. Finally, the study presents a robot design that leverages the most favorable workspace characteristics. The proposed methodology is validated through numerical simulations and experimental testing. The results demonstrate that the optimal workspace region exhibits superior dexterity and a reduced frequency of singular configurations, while the compliant chain effectively dampens vibrations. These findings confirm that the hybrid robot is well-suited for precision industrial applications. The source code for the workspace analysis and multi-objective optimization is made available online. This work offers valuable insights for the design of high-precision parallel-serial robot manipulators. kidney disease (CKD) has been constrained by the absence of high-quality, long-term data. This study aimed to characterize the complete life trajectories of CKD and its precursor, reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), by utilizing a comprehensive, high-resolution life course dataset. We analyzed 1,000 years of vital records from the Swedish Total Population (1808–1998), covering 100 million person-years. The data were segmented into 10-year age intervals, and life trajectories were calculated for both CKD and low eGFR. Hazard rates were computed for both conditions separately and in combination. Life trajectories revealed that CKD and low eGFR onset and mortality rates peaked between ages 60 and 70, with a secondary rise occurring between 80 and 90. The combined hazard rate for both conditions was 1.5 to 2 times higher than the sum of their individual rates, indicating a strong comorbidity. Furthermore, the joint hazard rate surpassed the individual rates for both conditions across all age groups. These findings suggest that CKD and low eGFR represent distinct phases of a shared life trajectory, characterized by a high proportion of individuals experiencing both conditions simultaneously. Additionally, the study identified a previously unrecognized life trajectory for CKD and low eGFR within the oldest old population (ages 80–90). These results underscore the necessity for further research into life trajectories in this age group to enhance our understanding of CKD epidemiology. Finally, the study demonstrates the potential of high-quality, long-term vital records for advancing life course epidemiology. (Am J Epidemiol. 2019;1–11)

The problem of finding a minimum-size $k$-dominating set is known as the $k$-domination problem. This study examines the $k$-dominating set problem within the framework of parameterized complexity. We demonstrate that $k$-dominating set is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) when parameterized by the solution size $d$, and we provide an explicit upper bound for its running time. Furthermore, we establish that $k$-dominating set is W[1]-hard when parameterized by the treewidth of $G$. The analysis also explores the impact of additional graph properties, such as bounded degree and bounded genus, on the problem's parameterized complexity. Finally, we present a polynomial-time algorithm for $k$-dominating set on chordal graphs, a result that extends to several other classes of chordal-like graphs. Additionally, we prove that the $k$-domination number can be computed in linear time for chordal graphs. These findings are derived from a more general algorithm applicable to $k$-dominating set on chordal graphs with missing cliques of size at most $m$, where $m$ is a fixed constant. This algorithm operates in $O(nm^m2^m)$ time and utilizes $O(m^m2^m)$ space. The approach is also applicable to a broader class of problems, including the $k$-center problem, $k$-path cover, and $k$-path packing. The primary methodology involves a novel application of the inclusion-exclusion principle to eliminate the need for an integer program. Additionally, we explore the relationship between $k$-dominating sets and the concept of $k$-kernelization. Specifically, we show that a $k$-dominating set can be found in linear time for graphs possessing a vertex cover of size $f(k)$, where $f(k)$ is a computable function of $k$. This result is achieved by first identifying a minimum vertex cover in $O(n)$ time and then applying the previously described algorithm. semantics of nondeterministic functional programming languages. This paper introduces q-powerdomains, which generalize the concept of powerdomains. The construction of these q-powerdomains is driven by the need to model the semantics of quantified computation, which encompasses not only standard nondeterminism but also higher-order probabilistic and other forms of quantified behavior. The paper also provides an alternative construction of powerdomains as a specific instance of this general approach. To define q-powerdomains, the paper relies on the framework of directed sets over q-domains, a concept that may be of independent interest. Finally, the paper explores the connections between the generalization of powerdomains and quantified computation. It demonstrates that the quantified data types studied by Plotkin can be viewed as q-powerdomains and that the probabilistic monad defined by Baez and Babich emerges as a specific instance of the q-powerdomain construction. Additionally, the paper establishes that the probabilistic monad possesses the same structural properties as q-powerdomains. In summary, this work aims to unify the understanding of powerdomains, their instances, and the type systems for quantified computation within a single, coherent framework. This study examines the dynamics of a warm, moist climate using a simplified model that incorporates water vapor, clouds, and convection. The model demonstrates that when the surface temperature rises above a critical threshold, the climate shifts from a cool state to a warm one. This transition is driven by the evaporation of surface water, which boosts water vapor content and latent heat release within the atmosphere. This process weakens the temperature gradient between the equator and the poles, thereby reducing the Hadley circulation. Consequently, the surface becomes drier in the cool state but wetter in the warm state. The model successfully replicates the characteristics of Earth's current climate and offers a novel explanation for the mechanism behind the warm-humid transition. Furthermore, it indicates that a warm-humid climate is more likely to evolve into a wet state, raising the possibility of significant flooding. These findings have significant implications for understanding Earth's climatic history and predicting future climate scenarios. The model is straightforward and can be solved analytically or via basic numerical methods. It is anticipated that these insights will prove valuable for both climate modeling and atmospheric theory. To address this, we introduce two approaches for computing the greatest post-fixpoints of a monotonic function $F$ on the complete lattice $\mathbb{L}^\bot = (\mathbb{L}, \sqsubseteq)$. The first method involves finding the least fixpoint of a function $G$ where $F$ and $G$ share the same iterations on $\mathbb{L$, meaning $\bigcup_{i\geq 0} F^i(\bot) = \bigcup_{i\geq 0} G^i(\bot)$. The second approach defines a function $H$ such that its $\omega$-iterations match those of $F$ on $\mathbb{L^\bot}$, satisfying $\bigcup_{i\geq 0} H^i(\bot) = \bigcup_{i\geq 0} F^i(\bot)$. We demonstrate that these two methods are equivalent and provide a technique for constructing both $G$ and $H$ from $F$. We then apply these methods to various aspects of (non-)termination analysis, including control-flow graphs for non-terminating programs, non-terminating traces in transition systems, and the termination proof policy within the (co)logic QTL. Furthermore, we extend these methods to compute greatest post-fixpoints for sub-distributive functions, which include those modeling the abstract interpretation of program semantics. Finally, we evaluate the practical utility of these methods by integrating them into the termination analyzer of the Prolog compiler, which is based on the (co)logic QTL. This integration enables the analysis of non-terminating functions that previously could not be handled. The resulting compiler, now equipped with this enhanced termination analyzer, is available at https://github.com/uni-tuebingen/proplog. Additionally, our methods are implemented in the termination analyzer of AProVE and are accessible at https://github.com/aprove/iterate. Both implementations are open source. (SNR) associated with the Galactic center's central star cluster, situated approximately 2.6 kiloparsecs from Earth. Its interior contains numerous young massive stars, including the famous Arches and Quintuplet clusters. This study aims to identify the physical origins of the X-ray emission observed within Sgr A East. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of the spectral and spatial characteristics of the X-ray data from the Chandra and XMM-Newton observatories. Our findings reveal that the X-ray emission is not uniform but consists of multiple distinct components. Specifically, we identified a bright, compact source located at the center of the remnant, which exhibits a hard spectrum and is likely linked to the energy generation mechanisms of the central star cluster. Additionally, we detected a diffuse, extended X-ray component with a softer spectrum that extends beyond the remnant's boundary. This extended emission may be attributable to the interaction between the SNR and the surrounding interstellar medium. These results offer valuable insights into the mechanisms driving the emission from Sgr A East. Furthermore, we conducted a search for gamma-ray emission from the remnant using data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT). Our analysis indicates that the gamma-ray emission is also spatially complex, comprising both a compact component and a diffuse component. The spectral analysis of the gamma-ray data yielded a photon index of $\gamma = 2.15 \pm 0.06 \pm 0.11$ (statistical $\pm$ systematic), which aligns with the spectral index derived from the X-ray data. Finally, we compared the gamma-ray emission from Sgr A East with that of other Galactic supernova remnants to better understand the nature of gamma-ray sources. These findings suggest that the gamma-ray emission from Sgr A East is likely dominated by hadronic processes. In summary, our findings provide a more detailed understanding of the physical origins of the emission from Sgr A East. These results will facilitate a deeper comprehension of the mechanisms responsible for the emission from this remnant and similar objects. Ultimately, this will contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of supernova remnant emission and the physical processes occurring within them. (Abridged)

to analyze the daily dynamics of COVID-19 cases in the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The monitoring system aggregates reports from various entities, including hospitals, laboratories, and public health authorities. We developed a model to forecast daily infection counts, which demonstrates high accuracy in predicting the actual number of new cases. Given the anticipated surge in infections due to the virus's exponential growth, we also created a forecast error model to quantify the uncertainty of these predictions. This methodology is applicable to any region where case reports are available daily. The forecast model is available as an open-source R package, accompanied by a detailed user manual. Consequently, we conclude that the most effective strategy to mitigate the pandemic is to reduce virus transmission, thereby lowering the total case count and minimizing the strain on the healthcare system. Finally, we propose that the proposed methods could serve as a valuable tool for public health authorities to inform the population and decision-makers to guide the management of the COVID-19 crisis. The analysis targets final states where each Higgs boson decays into a bottom quark pair, while the top quarks decay into W bosons and b quarks. The investigation examines associated production through both the $t\bar{t}hH$ channel, where the Higgs arises from $b$-quark loop-induced $t\bar{t}h$ associated production or vector boson fusion, and the $ttbhH$ channel, where the Higgs originates from $t\bar{t}h$ produced via vector boson fusion. The search employs a multivariate analysis technique to identify events with high jet multiplicity and multiple $b$-tagged jets. In the dominant $ttbhH$ channel, a significant excess of events is observed, suggesting the detection of Higgs pair production in association with a top quark pair. This finding is interpreted as setting the most stringent limit to date on the Higgs boson self-coupling, assuming a simplified model with only trilinear couplings. Furthermore, this represents the first observation of double Higgs production via any production mechanism. The measured signal strength is found to be 1.7 times the Standard Model prediction, with a corresponding 68% confidence level upper limit of 4.1 times the Standard Model prediction. Additionally, limits are established for various Beyond the Standard Model scenarios, including those involving anomalous trilinear Higgs couplings, additional Higgs bosons, and loop-induced production through new physics. The derived limits on the Higgs self-coupling and the Higgs trilinear coupling to a second Higgs boson are the most restrictive to date. Finally, constraints on the Wilson coefficients for dimension-6 operators in the Standard Model Effective Field Theory are updated. These results are based on the most comprehensive dataset and analysis methods to date, featuring novel techniques for handling high jet multiplicity and $b$-quark jet tagging. The methodology and findings will be presented at the 2023 CMS-ICHEP-EPAC-ATLAS-Novosibirsk-Workshop. The underlying data and analysis code are accessible via the CERN Open Data Portal. In reverse, by employing hypergeometric groups, we have successfully constructed K3 surface automorphisms with Siegel disks that achieve every possible Picard number within this range. These constructions rely on complex analytic methods, including hypergeometric differential equations, monodromy theory, and the Torelli theorem for K3 surfaces. A comparable approach has also yielded automorphisms with Siegel disks for del Pezzo surfaces of degrees 5 through 1. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Siegel disk automorphisms exist across a dense set within the moduli space of K3 surface automorphisms. This finding suggests that K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks are the generic case. Finally, we establish that the collection of K3 surface automorphisms with Siegel disks is invariant under the action of the automorphism group of the Lie algebra associated with a primitive affine automorphic representation. This last result extends a theorem by A. Borel, which originally concerned Kähler-Einstein K3 surfaces. The methodology employed to prove this result is expected to be applicable in other contexts, such as investigating hyperbolic geometry and automorphic representations. Additionally, we have constructed a hyperbolic geometric model for K3 surfaces with Siegel disk automorphisms, thereby generalizing a previous finding regarding Calabi-Yau manifolds. Our findings indicate that K3 surfaces with Siegel disk automorphisms exhibit significantly greater geometric complexity than those with polar actions. a supermassive dark matter halo can produce a detectable gamma-ray flux from dark matter annihilation, potentially explaining the recently identified excess in the GeV range observed by Fermi-LAT from the Galactic center. We show that this phenomenon is viable across a broad spectrum of neutralino parameters, contingent upon the neutralino's density profile. Furthermore, we establish that this scenario can be tested through dark matter searches targeting nuclear recoil and electron ionization signals. Specifically, we illustrate that a significant portion of the parameter space capable of reproducing the Galactic center gamma-ray excess is currently constrained by XENON1T and is further restricted by upcoming experiments. Additionally, we examine the impact of this scenario on the observed gamma-ray flux from the dwarf galaxy Willman 1, noting that the model remains compatible with that data provided the dark matter halo is not extremely dense. Finally, we argue that this framework offers a novel approach to addressing the small-scale structure issues inherent in the standard cold dark matter paradigm. We conclude that the possibility of dark matter being constituted by a neutralino with a non-trivial density profile should be considered in future dark matter research. It is established that the only such $n$-vertex well-covered split graphs that are not complete graphs possess vertex-induced component sizes of $(1,1,1,1,1,2)$ and $(1,1,1,1,2,3)$, respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for $n \geq 10$, these non-complete well-covered split graphs exhibit a vertex component structure of $(2,3)$, indicating that their non-maximal independent sets are induced by a vertex of size 2 and a set of size 3. Additionally, we examine the spectral properties of these well-covered split graphs. Specifically, let $A(G)$ denote the adjacency matrix of a graph $G$. We prove that if an $n$-vertex well-covered split graph $G$ (where $n \geq 10$) is not complete, then $G$ is not $k$-fold for any integer $k$ satisfying $-3 \leq k \leq 2$. Finally, we establish that the largest eigenvalue of an $n$-vertex well-covered split graph $G$ is at least $-2$ and at most $-1.618$. Notably, the lower bound of $-2$ is achieved exclusively by complete split graphs. These findings offer a more precise characterization of the eigenvalues for non-complete well-covered split graphs. As a direct consequence, we derive that the sum of the $k$ smallest eigenvalues of an $n$-vertex well-covered split graph $G$ is bounded below by $-2$ for $k=1,2,3,4,5,6$. This result aligns with the known spectral bound for non-complete well-covered graphs, which states that the sum of the $k$ smallest eigenvalues is at least $-k$ for $k=1,2,3,4,5$. Moreover, we provide a characterization of the spectral radius for well-covered split graphs and present several findings regarding the relationship between the well-coveredness of a graph and its contraction. We also explore the connection between the well-coveredness of a graph and its complement. Finally, we characterize the set of fold numbers for well-covered split graphs and determine the maximum number of well-covered split graphs that can be formed using $n$ vertices.

Furthermore, we show that the direction of this shape wave is determined by the object's handedness. Additionally, we find that the object's shape changes significantly influence the direction of the resulting propulsion. These findings offer a fresh perspective on the relationship between shape transformations and motility in two-dimensional fluids. Ultimately, our results indicate that an optimally twisted object can propel itself at a speed exceeding that of an object without any twist. These insights may prove valuable for designing autonomous robots capable of moving through complex, twisted environments. Furthermore, they may aid in understanding how biological cells twist to achieve efficient movement.
